vignette:
Dr. Robert Miller had been a steady presence—a calm, competent emergency physician who thrived under pressure. At sixty-three, he had spent over three decades in the trauma bay, believing he had seen everything. That belief was shattered on a Tuesday morning two years ago, during his commute into the city. The bus he rode every day was stopped by three armed men who boarded shouting orders. Robert was ordered to the floor, then commanded to tend to a wounded accomplice who had been shot during the initial takeover. He recalls the violence—the spray of blood, the screams, the rapid-fire instructions barked at him while he worked, hands shaking, trying to keep his own breathing even. For two hours he followed orders, treating one of the attackers as the others threatened passengers at gunpoint. When police finally breached the bus, Robert was released, physically unharmed, but something inside him had been dismantled.

In the weeks that followed, he could not stop scanning the rooms of his own home. Every creak of the floorboards, every rattle of the window frame made him freeze mid-step, certain someone had entered. He began lying awake at night listening—not to his wife Patricia’s breathing beside him, but to the faintest sounds beyond the bedroom door. He became convinced that the world was no longer safe, that any ordinary place—a grocery store, a waiting room, a quiet street—could suddenly turn hostile. What frightened him most was the realization that people were not what they seemed. The men on the bus had looked like anyone else before they pulled out their weapons. Now, when he passed strangers on the sidewalk, he studied their faces for signs of malice, for the subtle tension that might precede an explosion. But violence itself had become an unbearable trigger. Watching a movie with a fistfight, or even a television news report about a robbery, sent him into a cold sweat. In the ER, when a patient was wheeled in with a stab wound, he had to excuse himself to the staff bathroom, gripping the sink, his breath ragged, because the sight of blood from an assault—any assault—flooded him with the memory of the accomplice’s wound and the sound of a gun being racked.

The trigger that was hardest to avoid was public transport. He had always taken the bus to the hospital parking lot, but after the attack he could not bring himself to stand at a bus stop. The sight of a bus pulling to the curb sent his heart racing, his palms sweating. He started driving to work every day, an extra forty minutes each way through traffic that left him irritable before he even entered the hospital. Authority commands also became a minefield. When the chief of emergency gave him orders during a busy shift—"Start the fluids, page the attending, get the chart now"—Robert felt a flash of intense anger, a surge of defiance that he barely contained. More than once he snapped at nurses or residents for what he saw as unnecessary directives. His colleagues began to keep their distance, trading glances when he walked past. At home, Patricia bore the brunt of his irritability. If she asked him a simple question while he was reading, he would bark a response, then apologize rigidly. He felt constantly on guard, even in his own living room, as though an intruder might spring from behind the sofa. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed—not by any physical injury, but by the loss of the easy confidence he had once had. Medicine had been his calling; now he dreaded going to work, resenting the very environment that had once given him purpose. He avoided the hospital cafeteria where he had once eaten, because it was too exposed. He took the stairs instead of the elevator, because enclosed spaces made him feel trapped.

What finally brought Robert to seek help was a morning when he found himself screaming at a medical student for placing a stethoscope on the wrong spot, his voice echoing down the hall. Patricia had handed him a pamphlet for a trauma clinic and told him quietly that she couldn’t keep living like this. At sixty-three, he had been planning to retire in a few years, but now he wondered if he would even make it that long without losing his job or his marriage. Sitting in the waiting room, Robert is terrified that his career is slipping away, that his marriage might not survive his anger, and that he will never feel safe again. But beneath that fear, in a part of himself he had thought dormant, there is also a thin hope—the hope that someone might help him understand why he cannot stop listening, why he cannot trust anyone, and whether the man he used to be can ever be rebuilt.
